entries.title: Ned’s Club Is Buzzy, Exclusive — And a Work in Progress
entries.summary: Members say they enjoy the D.C. club for its uncommon amenities and upscale atmosphere. But how is the food?
entries.content:
Last year, a member of Ned’s Club who hadn’t had a drop of alcohol in years requested a zero-proof spritz at The Gallery, one of several dining rooms in Washington’s buzziest private club. He took one sip and tasted booze, a fact reconfirmed by his wife, and immediately informed his server about the full-strength mistake.

The attendant’s response took him aback: “Oh, well,” she said. “Nobody’s pregnant, are they?”

Zoom forward to an evening in late May. At the invitation of another member of Ned’s Club, I’m at The Gallery, with its marble-topped tables and Italian-influenced menu, when a fruit tart arrived in a circle of pink powdered … something. Dehydrated rhubarb or strawberries, maybe? Curious about the dusting on my plate, I asked the waiter what it was. “I have no idea,” he said, shaking his head as he hastily departed, incurious about getting an answer from a colleague.

No doubt you’ve heard about Ned’s Club, launched with fanfare across the top three floors of the historic Walker Building and American Security and Trust Company Building in February 2025. (Longtime Washingtonians might remember it as the former Riggs Bank; the name Ned’s Club is a hat tip to the architect behind the building that hosts the club’s London branch, Edwin Lutyens, who also designed the British Embassy in Washington.)

Billed by its principals as “a modern take on a traditional club,” the venue is owned by American billionaire investor Ron Burkle in a joint partnership with Michael Milken. It arrived at a time when the pace of exciting new restaurants in D.C. was approaching a turtle-like crawl and the city’s movers and shakers — young ones and women in particular — were hungrier than ever for something sexier and more approachable than what existed.

“You can’t just go back to your usual table at Tosca every other day,” a prominent female member of Ned’s Club told me, referencing the Italian-accented lobbyist draw downtown. Unlike the more established clubs in town, which cater to what she calls “SPM” — a “stale, pale and male” clientele, she translated — Ned’s Club reaches out to a wider audience.
DC0A7546 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Consider the admission fees. For most members, the upfront cost to join is $5,000, with an additional $5,000 fee annually. Food and drink are extra. Government workers are offered a different rate, as are communities that might not have the budget for exclusive club memberships.

“I’m a restaurant owner. I can’t afford a Ned,” says Tim Ma, the talent behind Tim Ma Hospitality, a co-founder of Chefs Stopping AAPI Hate — and the only member I interviewed who agreed to speak on the record about Ned’s Club. (The others fretted about their future relationship with the place.) Ma declined to share what he paid, but said the reduced cost made it “a no-brainer” to join.

Ned’s, the latest of a wave-lette of clubs catering to a cooler clientele, is onto something. Joiwind Ronen — hired as the executive director of membership and programs to put “a D.C. imprint on a global brand” — says Ned’s Club distinguishes itself from other private societies in part with diversity. A third of members are under 40, a third are in their 40s and a third are over 50, says Ronen, who adds that Ned’s Club is non-partisan. “I just introduced a Democratic governor and a member of the Trump administration in the elevator,” she sounds happy to report.

Not that Ned’s Club is all about welcoming huddled masses yearning to breathe free, provided they add some measure of flavor. Members of an exclusive, invitation-only group of power players pay $125,000 to join and $25,000 annually, for which they get access to the posh Founder’s Dining Room and concierge service at sibling clubs in Doha, London and New York. (Ronen wouldn’t share current membership numbers, but reports “we’ve had a wait list since we’ve opened” with 1,000 members.)

People sign on for myriad reasons: exclusivity, uncommon amenities, the opportunity to show off for out-of-towners or business associates as if they were in club-rich New York, members say.
Ned's Club (5464x6723, AR: 0.81)“It’s not as noisy as a coffee shop” and is a welcome convening spot, says the female club member, who appreciates the “well-curated space” and the fact that members can “go alone, and you always see someone you know.” Unlike at the more staid private clubs, “no one here asks, ‘Who’s your husband?’”

Reviews from members and their guests are mixed, however. “It’s not a cohesive experience,” one early joiner told me, describing how he once segued from drinks at the bar to a dining room, only to be asked at the host stand if he was a new member. “The flow isn’t right,” he says, particularly on the popular terrace on the top floor.

No one seems enthusiastic about the food. “It reads better than it tastes,” another member said, summing up his recent brunch experience at the Asian-themed Kaia, also on the top floor. “But you can’t beat outside on a nice day!”

Management receives feedback — yep, there’s an app for that — which probably explains a change of executive chefs in April and the arrival in July of a new food and beverage director.

The goal of Ned’s Club, says Ronen, is “to surprise and delight members,” and on the handsome surface, it delivers. Name another upscale watering hole with live music seven nights a week. Or consider the near-daily events programs that include lectures by Smithsonian curators and even off-site trips to Glenstone Gardens in Middleburg, Virginia, via a Bentley.
Ned's Club (10735x7921, AR: 1.36)Every member I’ve talked to agrees the space is a looker. The art on the walls, about 130 pieces, showcases the talent of women and locals; throughout, the fringed chairs and couches seem to offer hugs to their occupants. Palladian windows, lofty ceilings and soothing color schemes create a modern baronial look.

Worried about parking downtown? The club has you covered, with all-day valet service. “The convenience is huge,” says a freshly minted member, who finds it a “really comfortable place for coffee, a drink, a meeting.”

Not everybody’s buying. “It’s not as private as you hope,” an early subscriber told me. “Not when you go with a source and get seated next to Kellyanne Conway,” the former counselor to President Donald Trump.
Ned's Club (7071x4715, AR: 1.50)The member remains miffed that in The Library — basically an elegant WeWork that turns into a lounge at night — a server once ordered him to close his laptop at 5 p.m. while he was finishing an email. The member also thought it was ridiculous to pay an upcharge of “$4.50 for pickle juice for a martini” and questioned the status of customers. “It felt like a lot of strivers, third-year law associates you’ve never seen in your life.” Ultimately, this member says, “It never feels like home to me. I’m very happy not to rejoin.”

* * *

I’ve been hearing about the club since it opened. Until recently, however, I’d never stepped foot in the place. I’m not a member, and I needed to tag along with one to sample the whole gilded enchilada. Scheduling took some time (members who could be discreet are busy) but since April, when the new executive chef debuted, I managed to explore the club’s three dining rooms over the course of several months. I had some skin in the game: I enticed the four members who got me in with breakfasts, lunches and dinners that I personally paid for.

My guides coached me on what to expect. Dress-wise, almost anything goes. “Please no gym wear or baseball caps,” reads the club etiquette. (Ma shared that he was wearing a T-shirt the time he visited the Founder’s Dining Room, where he sat next to Milken, the club’s white-collar-criminal-turned-philanthropist landlord.)
DC0A7679 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Photography and phone calls are another matter. Even on the terrace, with its only-in-Washington vistas, photos and videos are verboten. The secretary of the treasury, a frequent visitor, can sip and sup in peace, in other words.

“We want our members to feel fully relaxed,” says Ronen, who admits it’s hard even for her not to take an occasional selfie. (Two servers told me they didn’t care if I snapped something quickly, but their managers would.) “I prefer no photos,” says an original member. “It gets people off their phone so they can face people in a conversation.” Calls are limited to the hallway or Ned’s two phone booths.

Every time I’ve checked in at the front desk, a host has taken my first name and last initial and placed a sticker on the lens of my phone. Then it’s up, up and away in a wood-paneled elevator.

I scored big and tall on my introduction to Ned’s Club: dinner in the exclusive Founder’s Dining Room, the steak and seafood restaurant on the 10th floor. As if the story gods were watching out for me, my party’s entrance coincided with Trump’s return from China on the South Lawn of the White House.

I watched as the helicopter blades from Marine One blasted surrounding trees while sharpshooters kept their eyes peeled from the roof of the residence — an impressive sight, no matter one’s political allegiance, and better in the company of prime rib ferried to the table on a shiny trolley. (Friday is Prime Rib Night here; $135 gets you roseate beef sliced tableside and an icy martini. Fun!)
Neds_04.jpg (11089x8192, AR: 1.35)Our gracious attendant tells us she previously worked at the upscale Bresca and Causa restaurants in Washington, and that the new executive chef, Joshua Smith, used to work for the acclaimed California chef Michael Mina, most recently at Bourbon Steak at the Four Seasons Las Vegas. Promising signs both.

What’s less enjoyable is the dull bread, the tinny background music and a draft from the air conditioning that feels as if we’re dining in a meat locker. (Bring a wrap.)

Surf — oysters on the half shell, a diver scallop capped with lemony cream sauce and shiny orange roe — trumps some of the other dishes, including a creamy gray steak tartare that lacks the expected sharpeners, arid chicken nesting on soft cabbage and a risotto that sits like Thanksgiving in the stomach. (The lobster on top is respectable.)

The side dishes are solid. Mashed potatoes are free of lumps. Creamed spinach is balanced with parmesan and garlic. And hot towels are a nice touch following the appetizers.

Ultimately, though, the restaurant doesn’t threaten the steak house pack in town. “Best for the view and the interior,” says the member who got me in with him. Gazing out on a postcard-perfect backdrop, including the colorfully illuminated Treasury Building, I nod in agreement. Indeed, my loftiest memory about that night is the price tag: just over $1,000 for four, not including a round of drinks we had in the bar out front.

“‘You don’t really go there for the food,’” a new member says he was told by other members. “There’s some truth to that.” His words play in my head throughout my next two visits to the club, where I dine twice in The Gallery. (Smith oversees the kitchen staff for all three dining rooms)
Neds_Club_07b.jpg (14090x6637, AR: 2.12)First thought: What a snooze of a menu! Judging from the tuna crudo, tomato soup, rigatoni Bolognese, grilled salmon (are you falling asleep yet?) and New York strip steak, the generic selections could have been assembled by AI.

Second impression: Someone’s not tasting the food. The swordfish is thick and juicy, but those compliments are undone by a topper of peppers and olives that go down like a salt lick. It’s the same problem with orecchiette piled with a blizzard of toasted breadcrumbs and gloppy wisps of Swiss chard. The aforementioned fruit tart with the mystery garnish traps rhubarb and strawberries in a doughy crust that bends, rather than flakes. I dig the thyme-buttermilk ice cream, though.

The reason food critics go out to eat with companions, often multiple times, is so they can sample the range of a script. And so I did. In a city stuffed with good pizza, The Gallery’s oval pepperoni pie is fine, with a crust that’s by turns crisp and pillowy. There’s a sea of fried calamari out there, but I found my fingers darting back, again and again, to a pile of bronzed crisp rings and tentacles scattered with crimson fresno chiles.

* * *

One thing I’ve learned over decades of restaurant-hopping is this: People will put up with middling food if the service is good. No matter how delicious the cooking, though, no one wants to feel overlooked or unwelcome. Ned’s Club members were quick to tell me about the inconsistent or absent service throughout the club.

I observed plenty of ineptitude in their presence. One evening at Kaia, the food arrived before fresh plates did, a second bottle of wine was unceremoniously poured into used glasses and no one seemed able to multitask. Faced with a sad heap of shredded duck leg with the texture of beef jerky, some dry scallions and stiff pancakes, I asked if there was supposed to be hoisin sauce for the sharable entree. “Oh yeah,” a server said, after we were already a few bites into the $55 travesty. As we ate the self-made wraps, it sounded like footsteps on gravel in my mouth. Crunch, crunch, crunch. Bon appetite, gang!

To be fair, the sushi and steamed pork-and-prawn dumplings are fair, and I ate most of an appetizer of craggy hot chicken nuggets, cooled with a dunk of yuzu-brightened mayonnaise. But the steamed cod leans sweet, and it isn’t the silken fish you hope for, and a side of Brussels sprouts proves sodden and cloying.

A week earlier, at the bar on the popular terrace, I was told the cocktail I requested was from an old menu, unavailable. Funny to see the same drink, then, on the current menu on this particular visit.

Another night on the rooftop terrace, three waters were dropped off for four people, only two of three people got their drinks together, and we all watched as a member strode past our table, grumbling that she was off to find the cocktails her party ordered “30 minutes ago.” The fog of a nearby cigar smoker enveloped our space; the club’s starry views can come at a price.
Neds_05.jpg (5464x6706, AR: 0.81)Breakfast, served in The Gallery, is the club’s fastest-growing meal, and I was delighted on my last trip to find chilaquiles on the menu. Buttery pieces of avocado and a textbook-perfect fried egg on a base of refried beans and fried tortilla made an ideal eye-opener. A view of the Washington Monument on a sunny day enhanced the fresh berries and crisp waffle, too. No one bothered to ask if we wanted more coffee, though.

“They’re fixing pieces, but not at the same time,” said the member who got the alcohol-laced drink rather than the mocktail. He told me this over a lunch that was better than my dinners at The Gallery. I can vouch for a messy-but-tasty smashburger under a glossy potato bun, a prettier-than-before tuna crudo anointed with basil oil, and a congenial waiter who poured my club soda with bitters at the table. Smith has obviously been tweaking and editing.

“Food is central to how members connect, gather and experience the Club,” read a press release from Ned’s Club in April.

I couldn’t agree more. The views and decor can’t do all the work. Which is why I felt a tinge of disappointment during my recent breakfast, when I inquired about “Chef Dan’s bread,” pointing out the shoutout on the menu to a server. She replied with a smile and a shrug; clearly, she had no idea who he was.
entries.author: Tom Sietsema

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Where to Go for D.C.’s Restaurant Week
entries.summary: Plus a dining guide to Napa Valley, and the trouble with front-of-house service.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross, and solve your pressing restaurant queries.

Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space. Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

As we approach Restaurant Week in D.C., what restaurants (hidden gems or expensive splurges) would you recommend? 

The goal of the popular promotion, run by the Restaurant Association Metropolitan Washington, is to get diners into restaurants at a time when they are traditionally slow, using good value as a carrot. From Aug. 24 through Aug. 30, the 200-plus participants will offer multicourse lunches and brunches between $25 and $35 and dinners in tiers of $40, $55 and $65, depending on the restaurants’ ambitions.

I advise people to try places they have yet to splurge on, to reserve a table as early as possible, and go earlier in the week — because the choice restaurants book fast for weekends and service tends to be less rushed Sunday through Tuesday.

You’ll want to preview the menus, too. Smart restaurants create three-course lists that feature dishes they tend to regularly serve, not simply less pricey selections. And cool customers will tip like it’s a normal night out (and not ask for modifications).

My top recommendations this season span a world of flavors. For dinners, consider the lively Peruvian draw Amazonia in Blagden Alley ($65); the handsome Bombay Club near the White House ($55); Ceibo, a friendly source of Uruguayan fare in Adams Morgan ($65), where I never pass on the chorizo dumplings; Del Mar at the Wharf ($55) for a refined taste of Spain from the acclaimed chef Fabio Trabocchi; the typically serene Onggi offering sublime Korean in Dupont Circle (which offers three different tier-priced menus, from $40 to $65); and the alluring Dabney in Shaw for a survey of the Mid-Atlantic ($65).
DSC04473 copy.jpg (2336x2804, AR: 0.83)Hidden gems don’t stay secrets the way they used to, alas, but if you’re looking for a fresh face in the crowd, there’s the modern Filipino storefront Kayu in Dupont Circle, where chef Paolo Dungca will be serving crab noodles, pork with peach barbecue sauce, and a vegetarian assembly of caraflex cabbage, summer squash and burnt coconut among his main course options ($65).

Increasingly, in mid- and top-tier restaurants alike, I find restaurants aren’t hiring or training front-of-the-house staff that understand they’re in the business of service, making customers feel welcome. 

Restaurants tell me they’re still dealing with the aftermath of the pandemic, when so many skilled veterans left the industry and operators needed to replace their ranks, often with people who had no service experience.

In general, once diners are seated, they should expect within the first minute or two a menu, water, and a greeting, even a short one if the restaurant is busy: “Thanks for joining us. I’ll be with you in a moment.” (Anyone who flies a lot can tell you during a delay, they’d rather hear straight talk from a pilot than no update at all. Same goes for anyone who has to wait for a table in the entrance of a dining room.)

Veteran New York restaurateur Danny Meyer, whose restaurants within the Union Square Hospitality Group are revered for their attention to diners, calls hospitality a team sport. He looks for a handful of specific traits when he recruits: genuine warmth, a hunger to learn, strong work ethic, self-awareness, empathy and integrity. As for prior experience, “Resumes are the least important part of the hiring process,” he’s famously written. “I’m looking for a twinkle in the eye.” The best way to clear a table or withdraw a cork from a wine bottle can be learned, in other words. Natural warmth is more of a challenge.

I like to think hospitality is a two-way street, by the way, and that diners can make or break a good time. Not to get all Mr. Rogers, but it helps to enter a restaurant with a smile and the belief you’re going to have a positive experience. Invariably, staff respond accordingly.

I love a starry dining experience, but I want to load my Napa Valley trip with awesome foodie experiences outside of the Michelin guide. Your recommendations, please?

It’s been a minute since I’ve eaten widely in my former stomping grounds, but that just gave me an opportunity to check in with some chowhounds I trust, including a longtime reader of mine, Robert Mandel, who resides in Sonoma but eats out widely. His response was a mile long (thank you, sir!), so I pared down the lot to about a week’s worth of (solid, casual) choices, then mixed in picks from my Bay Area critic pals along with some fond dining memories of my own.

You want to check out:

Slanted Door in Napa: The original modern Vietnamese restaurant was an institution in San Francisco. Home in on the imperial rolls, chili-caramel chicken clay pot, and shaking beef.

Mustards Grill in Napa: Chef Cindy Pawlcyn’s decades-old roadhouse, featuring an on-site organic garden and a you’re-in-California script, is as beloved and bustling a restaurant as they come in wine country. Check out the signature Mongolian pork chop and lofty lemon-lime tart.

Ciccio in Yountville: Housed in a century-old former Italian grocery store, the edible draws include meatball-plumped peppers, gnocchi with cod and scallops, and pizzas from a wood-burning oven. The owners feature wines they produce themselves at Altamura Vineyards and Winery.

Oxbow Public Market in Napa: A grazer’s banquet, the 40,000 square foot food hall, located along the Napa River, includes goods from Ritual Coffee Roasters, Fatted Calf, and Hog Island Oyster Co. Make time for a seasonal pour-over, a muffuletta crammed with house-made meats, and a platter of locally harvested oysters.

Carabao in Napa: Set off with farmer hats suspended from the ceiling and named for a water buffalo recognized for its power, the snug Caraboa represents Napa Valley’s first Filipino eatery. Specialities include pork lumpia, kare-kare and, this being California, sisig tacos.

Tarla Mediterranean Bar + Grill in Napa: Tarla “is my favorite restaurant in the town of Napa. They bill themselves as a Mediterranean restaurant, and they are, but think the best Turkish and Lebanese,” says Mandel, my wine country tipster. Popular for its happy hour during the week, where diners get discounts on signature small plates — a trio of Greek dips with warm pita is $11 — and glasses of vino for $8. Pro tip: no corkage fee on Tuesdays.

Market in St. Helena: “Market is a wonderful spot to escape all the chi-chi Napa joints,” says Mandel. “It is comfort food defined.” Market has long been a watering hole for winemakers. “I once saw Robert Mondavi dining with a friend there,” says my correspondent.

Zuzu in Napa: The convivial, indoor-outdoor tapas retreat offers paella in addition to Spanish small plates: garlic soup with chorizo, salt cod drizzled with California olive oil, seared pork cheeks and braised tongue with persimmons and more. “José Andrés would be very happy here,” my guide writes.

Wilfred’s Lounge in Napa: What to drink with coconut shrimp, Spam musubi and poke bowls? Probably a bahama mama, among other attractions at Napa’s sole tiki bar, popular for its live music.

I’m not a big planner when I’m on the road. Short of Googling or asking Claude, what are your tips for eating well in unfamiliar places? 

Knowing what to avoid is crucial. I tend to steer clear of restaurants with buses parked out front, almost always a sign of a tourist trap; posted reviews older than a year or two; dining rooms that smell off (say, with cleaning fluid) or devoid of any pleasant cooking aroma. I’ve been known to walk in, and right out of, restaurants where staff or diners or both look sullen. I also pass on places where someone is hawking menus outside (think South Beach) and lists are written in more than two languages.

Away from home, keep your eyes open for signs on the road flagging a fire station supper, a crab feast, or a Greek church bake sale. All the better if the signs are hand-written.

Pose the right question to the right local. “What’s the best restaurant around?” tends to get you a fancy (read: expensive or exclusive) response. “Where would you go if you were leaving town for a while?” generally elicits something beloved. Here in the U.S. and abroad, I’ve found some of the best tipsters working in book stores, antique shops and quality food markets.

Finally, following a memorable meal out, I invariably ask my server, sommelier, or chef where they would eat on their night off. Good knows good.

I need a place for the occasional “bite to eat.” Not a dive, but not fine dining, either.

My Goldilocks recommendation at the moment is The Grace, recently introduced by chef Sanjay Mandhaiya, the owner of Karravaan and Pappe in D.C., and the successor to the popular Passenger in Shaw. The attractive, two-story restaurant beckons with a menu of sandwiches and salads on the ground floor and a slightly elevated list upstairs, although a server informed us all the food is available throughout the space, which Mandhaiya calls “a modern tavern with elevated food.”

Wherever you land, you’ll want to start with some broiled oysters, swabbed with collard green butter, and crisp fried sweet-and-tangy cauliflower before moving on to bigger plates — maybe a burger, compact but flavorful, and paired with thick french fries dusted with Parmesan. Garlic-scented linguine with tender scallops, draped with a creamy wine sauce, would be better without chewy bites of lobster.

The name was chosen to highlight a feminine look — floral restrooms, velvet walls — and the kitchen is led by Courtney Evans, who comes to D.C. from Charlotte. (Fans of “Next Gen Chef” on Netflix might recognize her as a former contestant.)

Two of us recently sat at a wood counter shaped like the state of Minnesota on Zepbound (it’s skinny) on the second floor, in view of a dining room warmed with amber lights and local art, where we sipped a stinging, mezcal-fueled Pepper & Corn cocktail and basked in friendly attention. Night owls should know they have another place to eat late at night. The kitchen at Grace, while closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, otherwise stays open til 1:30 a.m., and alcohol flows till 2 a.m. weekdays and 3 a.m. weekends. Don’t be surprised to rub elbows with members of the industry after they get off their shifts.
entries.author: Tom Sietsema

entries.title: Trump’s Claims About Combating Crime Are Based on Skewed Data
entries.summary: A Trump administration release lauding federal interventions last year made false claims about how much the cities improved.
entries.content:
The White House misrepresented and exaggerated a recent crime report to overstate the impact of last summer’s federal intervention in four cities, according to a NOTUS review.

On July 23, the Council on Criminal Justice, a nonpartisan criminal justice policy organization, released a report on crime in several cities. Days later, the White House cited the report in a news release touting President Donald Trump’s record on public safety. In the release, the White House claimed that the greatest turnaround was seen in four cities where Trump sent federal agency officials and National Guard troops — a claim the data didn’t support. And two of the four cities the White House mentioned — Memphis and New Orleans — weren’t even included in the CCJ report cited in the White House’s release.

The White House claimed that, “The steepest homicide drops have come in cities where the Trump Administration stepped in after Democrat leaders failed to act,” specifically listing Memphis, New Orleans, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. But the steepest homicide drops weren’t in those four cities, according to Ernesto Lopez, the CCJ senior researcher who co-wrote the report.

Lincoln, Nebraska, had the steepest drop. Washington, D.C., had the sixth steepest, Los Angeles the 17th, and Memphis and New Orleans weren’t included in the report.

The report used data from 36 cities to display the short- and long-term shift in crime that began in the second half of 2022, Lopez said. The authors excluded Memphis due to statistical anomalies. Lopez could not recall if New Orleans had been included in previous iterations of the report.

Supporting data was included in the White House release for Memphis and New Orleans from a separate source, a July Substack article by crime data analyst Jeff Asher. Asher calculated that the Memphis homicide rate had fallen by 43.3% in 2026 from 2025, with New Orleans down 32.1%. (In his 2025 mid-year report, Memphis’ and New Orleans’ murder rates were down 15.1% and 27.4%, respectively, from 2024.) Fort Worth, Texas, had the steepest drop in Asher’s 2026 report, with Memphis just behind and New Orleans in ninth.

On Monday, Asher called the White House’s claim an “incorrect statement.”

“I don’t necessarily think it fully reflects what’s in the piece that I’ve written,” Asher, the co-founder of AH Datalytics, told NOTUS.

“President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement on Tuesday. “Just today, another survey by the Major Cities Chiefs Association found significant drops in violent crime including a more than 17% decrease in murders. Unlike Defund-the-Police Democrats, President Trump will always stand with our law enforcement officers and deliver safer American neighborhoods.”

After sending the statement to NOTUS, the White House published a news release featuring the survey from the Major Cities Chiefs Association, displaying the cities with the largest drops in homicides. D.C. and Memphis were ninth and 10th for the largest drops, respectively, according to an analysis by Axios.
Federal Enforcement Cities Memphis (5105x3404, AR: 1.50)
The White House release used the CCJ report as a reference for most of the press release’s takeaways before pivoting away from it to claim cities that Trump sent federal troops to had the greatest change in murder rate.

Homicides are on track to reach a historically low level in 2026, and officials in Memphis and New Orleans have shared credit with Trump. In January, New Orleans Police Superintendent Anne Kirkpatrick cited the National Guard’s presence as a crime deterrent.

“We’re just grateful that crime is down, and I don’t care who gets the credit,” Kirkpatrick said at the time.

The CCJ report didn’t delve into potential causes for the downward trend. But both Asher and Andrew Wheeler, a crime data analyst who founded the website CRIME De-Coder, pointed to the broader decline that’s been ongoing since former President Joe Biden’s administration.

After a spike that followed the COVID-19 pandemic and George Floyd protests, crime “has been dropping down pretty consistently across the U.S.,” Wheeler said.

“It isn’t like something that just started like a few months ago or anything like that. It’s been pretty consistent over several years at this point,” he added.

Asher pointed to the Bourbon Street terrorist attack on New Year’s Day in 2025 as an example of how some crime reductions couldn’t be credited to Trump’s actions. The number of people killed in the attack — 14 — skewed the city’s murder rate for the rest of the year, he said. If the attack wasn’t included in the city’s crime data, its 2025 and 2026 murder rates would be similar.
New Orleans Mardi Gras (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)The White House’s release was published during a stretch when Trump’s approval rating has sunk to 38% or lower in multiple surveys, as he deals with the ongoing Iran war that has spurred higher prices in the grocery store and at the gas pump. Given the improving crime rates, the White House has emphasized the issue. A July Economist/YouGov poll found that Trump’s approval on crime outpaced his overall approval rating, 41% to 36%. On Monday, the administration released statistics about crime improvements in D.C. one year after the institution of the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Again Task Force.

Mayor Muriel Bowser said Monday the continued presence of out-of-state National Guard troops in D.C. is “problematic.”

Since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he has dedicated significant effort into the beautification of America’s cities. The emphasis birthed the federal task force in Memphis and troops in Los Angeles, New Orleans and D.C., where his infatuation with aesthetics matured into renovations, freshly gilded statues and fixed park fountains.

Although the National Guard remains active in Memphis, New Orleans and D.C., Trump has turned his attention away from sending troops into Democratic-led cities — but the cities remain on his mind. During a speech last week in Las Vegas, Trump said, “The cities stink. They smell. The sidewalks are loaded with horrible stuff.”

entries.title: ‘There’s a fatigue’: Iran Grates on Republicans As Midterms Near
entries.summary: “There’s a lot of confusion,” said Sen. John Kennedy, who directed his complaints to Vice President Vance recently.
entries.content:
Back in March, Senate Republicans were hopeful the war in Iran would last only a matter of weeks — a limited operation that would allow gas prices to fall back in place and avoid the prospect of a conflict dragging closer to the midterm elections.

Nearly six months on, the protracted war has thoroughly vexed President Donald Trump and administration officials as they try to bring it to an end. It also means Republican lawmakers are being pressed regularly to explain the strategy.

“We get a lot of calls about it into the office. They’re just wearing out on it,” said West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, a member of Republican leadership, adding that the timeline has become the war’s most problematic part for constituents.

“We’ve done this before where we’ve had very elongated engagements,” Capito said. “People don’t want to see that. They don’t want to see boots on the ground. They don’t want to see our money going there. There’s a fatigue factor, for sure.”

The administration has been seeking an off-ramp for months, especially amid reports that U.S. munitions are dwindling rapidly. Officials pointed to a “memorandum of understanding” that was agreed to in mid-June, but the framework was effectively dead only weeks later after fighting reignited when commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz were fired upon by Iranian forces.

Most recently, Iran said it would only allow American ships to navigate freely through the strait if the U.S. met a series of high demands. Among those were billions of dollars in U.S. payments, the end of the naval blockade and the exit of U.S. troops from the region.

This has put Trump and the administration in a tough position as they work for a deal to reopen the strait for business — which has become the main priority ahead of November. But lawmakers believe the roller-coaster nature of the war and the negotiations to bring it to a halt aren’t doing them any favors.

“I wish the president were more clear about what his objectives are,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said. “This off again, on again [cadence] is creating some confusion in people’s minds.”

Cornyn argued that the weekslong timeline laid out by the administration at the outset was a mistake in itself.

“The enemy always gets a vote. That’s the problem with providing timetables and deadlines in a military conflict,” he said.

The war is also colliding with Election Day, less than three months out, something Republicans who wanted the war wrapped up prior to the summer warned about when it was launched in February.

According to a recent Reuters/Ipsos survey, only 35 percent said they approve of the U.S. strikes against Iran, with only 17 percent saying that stability in the Middle East will get better over the next year

Consumers are also still being hit with high gas prices, which sit around $4 per gallon on average — about a dollar more than at the start of the war.

Few believe that figure will improve. Fifty-eight percent of respondents said they believe gas prices will worsen.

And the public doesn’t understand the endgame. Sixty-nine percent said in a previous Reuters/Ipsos poll that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals” of the military effort in Iran.

For now, the White House is trying to take an alternate tact after months of threatening to wipe Iran off the earth at times.

“We are low-keying it,” Trump told Axios recently. “We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.”

“It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game,” Trump said of the back-and-forth with Iran.

Adding to the frustrations for lawmakers has been a lack of briefings from the administration. Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, told reporters he couldn’t remember the last time he received a briefing from the Pentagon regarding the war.

“It’s not recent and it’s not frequent or routine,” he told reporters.

But as the Senate tackled the final week pile-up before the summer recess, Iran was the dominant subject when Vice President JD Vance attended a Senate Republican luncheon.

According to members, Vance was peppered with questions about the conflict, with some urging the administration to be more transparent.

Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy suggested he and other officials hold a news conference “and spend all day talking straight up to the American people about where we are, why we went in, what the hold up is, how much damage has been done to Iran, what we know about their nuclear stockpiles, what we think about the strait.”

He told reporters he thought “there’s a lot of confusion about Iran.” And, Kennedy admitted, “I wish the American people could have heard what the vice president told us.”

entries.title: D.C.’s Buzziest Private Club
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for August 13, 2026.  You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Ned’s Club is buzzy, exclusive — and a work in progress, writes NOTUS food correspondent Tom Sietsema.

Unlike the more established clubs in town, Ned’s reaches a wider audience. The upfront membership cost for most is $5,000, with an additional $5,000 fee annually. The result? A third of its members are under 40, a third are in their 40s and a third are over 50. The nonpartisan club has had a waitlist since it launched in February 2025 with 1,000 members, and boasts a cool clientele.

“I just introduced a Democratic governor and a member of the Trump administration in the elevator,” the club’s executive director of membership and programs told NOTUS.

Members say they love the uncommon amenities, the private atmosphere and the postcard views. But what about the food?

“It reads better than it tastes,” one member said. “But you can’t beat outside on a nice day!”

Across three trips (accompanied by members, of course), Tom found the dining experience to be a mixed bag. Breakfast was good, the sushi was fair and the service was, at times, inept. Food and drink are not included in a membership, and often come with a heavy price tag: Tom’s dinner for four in the exclusive Founders Dining Room ran to just over $1,000.

“‘You don’t really go there for the food,’” a new member says he was told by other members. “There’s some truth to that.”

DC0A7679 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)




DEEP DIVE

Ward 8 council member Trayon White’s federal bribery trial kicks off next month, and new court filings this week offer insights into the case prosecutors hope to make and the defense White’s attorney is expected to mount.

For prosecutors, the case is simple. They say that in 2024, White accepted bribes from Allieu Kamara, a local businessman who wanted to secure more contracts with the city. The exchanges were caught on video, and prosecutors allege White gambled away the proceeds at a local casino.

White’s defense attorney aims to poke holes in those accusations, arguing that the multi-term lawmaker didn’t do anything to actually help Kamara, and that he may actually be the victim of entrapment.

A federal judge will soon rule on final motions ahead of the trial, including whether White can openly argue that he was entrapped and whether prosecutors can show jurors pictures of trips White and Kamara took together to the Dominican Republic.

Should White be convicted, he could face more than a decade in prison, and he’d be immediately expelled from the council. That would trigger a special election early next year to fill the seat representing many of D.C.’s poorest neighborhoods.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A D.C. police lieutenant pleaded guilty last week to two felony counts of solicitation of a minor after being caught in a child-sex-abuse sting operation recorded on “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” WTOP reports.

The Trump administration plans to spend at least $900 million — much of it taxpayer money — on White House construction projects, The Washington Post reports.

A former D.C. liquor license inspector has been fined $6,000 for threatening a local watering hole with additional inspections and fines if it didn’t reduce or forgive his bar tabs. The inspector, Jeremy Zollarcoffer, left the Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration in April.

In a rare move, the Justice Department has convened a special grand jury in D.C. to be overseen by one of U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s top allies, The Washington Post reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Great snakes! Prince George’s County police have charged three people with stealing more than 60 reptiles from Virginia and Maryland pet stores, ABC7 reports.





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

As we approach Restaurant Week in D.C., what restaurants (hidden gems or expensive splurges) would you recommend?

My top recommendations this season span a world of flavors. For dinners, consider the lively Peruvian draw Amazonia in Blagden Alley ($65); the handsome Bombay Club near the White House ($55); Ceibo, a friendly source of Uruguayan fare in Adams Morgan ($65), where I never pass on the chorizo dumplings; Del Mar at The Wharf ($55) for a refined taste of Spain from the acclaimed chef Fabio Trabocchi; the typically serene Onggi offering sublime Korean in Dupont Circle (which offers three different tier-priced menus, from $40 to $65); and the alluring Dabney in Shaw for a survey of the mid-Atlantic ($65).

Hidden gems don’t stay secrets the way they used to, alas, but if you’re looking for a fresh face in the crowd, there’s the modern Filipino storefront Kayu in Dupont Circle, where chef Paolo Dungca will be serving crab noodles, pork with peach barbecue sauce and a vegetarian assembly of caraflex cabbage, summer squash and burnt coconut among his main course options ($65).

In the full Q&A: hospitality as a two-way street, how to eat well in an unfamiliar place and a foodie’s guide to Napa Valley.  





SPORTS

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders mostly manhandled the Dolphins in the team’s first joint practice session Wednesday in Ashburn. Facing another team for the first time this summer, Washington played with aggression on both sides of the ball. The two teams will face off again in a more official capacity on Friday in the first preseason game.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Cubs, 4:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics at Aces, 10 p.m. (Amazon Prime)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

entries.title: General Concerns
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What comes after the primaries. Elizabeth Warren crosses the aisle. Double-checking White House crime stats. Tom Sietsema reviews The Ned. And: buying nuclear. 





THE LATEST

Let’s pivot to the general, shall we? In 82 days, the midterm election will be officially here.

If it’s been a minute since you thought about it, let us catch you up. News cycle after news cycle brought Democratic tea parties, campaigns imploding under scandal, tests of Donald Trump’s endorsement power, debating the importance of TV ad buys, learning who Hasan Piker is, polling-pocalypses and all other the fun (or: “fun”) stuff the primaries have been about. After all that, the general election is still about the same thing it was the last time you checked: prices.

Call it affordability, call it the economy, stupid, call it whatever you want. Just make sure you call it salient. Surveys show over and over: Voters want to know how their electeds will make things cheaper.

Politicians are more clued into this than some might think. Before they left town, NOTUS’ Manuela Silva asked senators the one word they thought would define the election. “Economy,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina). “Affordability,” said Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah). “Costs,” said Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota).

“Gas,” said Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas). “I can’t say, ‘cost of gas’?” We’ll allow it.

Shifting the conversation to prices is crucial to any midterm strategy. Democrats say they can do it easily, pointing to drama-free unity rallies and the surge of voters turning out for all types of Democrats this year as evidence they can put messy primaries behind them quickly. Besides, a good deal of primary season ads were about prices. But it was sometimes quite nasty out there, with ideological purity tests dominating many races. Can all that be back-burnered until the party’s traditional circular firing squad returns to prominence, 30 seconds or so after the November polls close?

Republicans have a different challenge: the toll of the Iran war and how much voters don’t like it. “We get a lot of calls about it into the office. They’re just wearing out on it,” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) told NOTUS’ Al Weaver. “They don’t want to see boots on the ground. They don’t want to see our money going there.” It’s hard to move on from something that is still happening, especially when it affects the cost of gas.

Open tabs: Trump administration again urges Supreme Court intervention on mail ballots (Reuters); The backlash to social media bans has already begun (Politico); Lawsuit seeks to ban Trump Media from charging for early access to president’s posts on US policy (AP); Take a look at Trump’s Kennedy Center renovation plans (Axios)





From the Hill


Republican senators’ favorite Democrat? No, it’s not Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren has worked on a slew of bipartisan populist legislation co-sponsored by the likes of Republican Sens. Josh Hawley of Missouri and Bernie Moreno of Ohio — not generally seen as among their party’s ideological squishes, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports. “We have a great work relationship,” Hawley said about Warren.

From the White House


Karoline Leavitt’s exit: The president’s press secretary says she’s leaving the gig for greener pastures. That kicked off a round of D.C. gossip reasoned speculation about who might take the briefing-room lectern next. One person close to the White House told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright that her replacement would almost certainly come from outside and not from the current press office.

Running the numbers: The White House misrepresented and exaggerated a recent crime report to overstate the impact of last summer’s federal intervention in four cities, NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports. The White House cited a Council on Criminal Justice report to say drops in homicides were most pronounced in cities where Trump has surged federal agents. But the underlying data doesn’t support that claim.

“President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that,” a White House spokesperson responded.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: Ned’s Club Is Buzzy, Exclusive — And a Work in Progress, by Tom Sietsema

Also, from Sietsema: Talk to Tom: Where to Go for D.C.’s Restaurant Week

Sports desk: Commanders Show Few Weaknesses in Joint Practice With Dolphins, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

The president’s nuclear portfolio: Trump has invested between $6.4 million and $19.45 million in U.S. nuclear technology companies or utility companies that operate nuclear reactors, NOTUS’ Jade Lozada reports. These holdings stand to pay off big if Trump’s promise to dramatically expand nuclear power generation in America comes to pass.

The two things have a close connection — the administration’s nuclear campaign kicked off last May, with Trump signing four executive orders favorable to the industry. Within three weeks, Trump acquired between $114,000 and $485,000 of stock in energy companies with nuclear facilities, including several five-figure purchases on the same day.

More: ICE Wants to Give Agents Gloves That Deliver Electric Shocks, by Manuela Silva

Energy Department Abandons Biden-Era Plans for More Power Lines, by Anna Kramer and Mara Hoplamazian

Rep. Max Miller’s Ex-Wife Sues Him Over Photo He Shared of Their Daughter, by Jenna Monnin

A Small Texas Law Firm Backs Out of HHS Contract After Backlash, by Manuela Silva





NOT US

  • Inside the White House bet that Netanyahu’s peace plan rejection is for show, by Myah Ward and Megan Messerly for Politico
  • Mamdani’s Honeymoon With New York Is Over, by James Fanelli for The Wall Street Journal
  • Hong’s defeat shows the left evolving further away from 2020, by David Weigel for Semafor




BE SOCIAL

entries.title: Trump Is Personally Invested in His Push to Boost the Nuclear Industry
entries.summary: The president owned between $6.4 million and $19.45 million in U.S. companies tied to nuclear energy at the end of 2025, according to his financial disclosure.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump could stand to profit from his administration’s unprecedented investments into the nuclear energy industry.

Trump has invested between $6.4 million and $19.45 million in U.S. nuclear technology companies or utility companies that operate nuclear reactors, according to a NOTUS review of his 2025 personal financial disclosure. Trump’s holdings could reap significant gains as his administration seeks to rapidly expand the nuclear industry.

Trump’s investment portfolio includes stocks from the nuclear industry’s major players among utilities, broadening the possibility for profit even as it remains unclear the extent to which companies may leverage the administration’s deregulatory environment to bet big on nuclear.

The president owns between $2.7 million and $11.5 million in Duke Energy, which operates 11 nuclear units across North and South Carolina. The president holds anywhere from $667,000 to $1.4 million in Constellation Energy, the largest nuclear operator in the U.S., and purchased as much as $1.1 million of the company’s stock in 2025. Federal elected officials are only required to report their assets in broad ranges.

Trump purchased between $4.8 million and $12.9 million in energy stock last year as the administration launched its ambitious policy and funding campaign to scale the country’s limited nuclear power facilities into the next big clean energy source.

His stakes in these companies represent a sliver of his vast investment portfolio, which totals at least $858 million, according to his 927-page financial disclosure. Trump’s broad exposure to the U.S. economy leaves few, if any, sectors his policies wouldn’t touch, raising concerns among ethics experts about how the president profits off his administration’s work.

Trump and his family’s finances coalesced around nuclear start-ups as his energy agenda ramped up last year.

The Trump administration’s latest deal would allow U.S. energy companies to develop nuclear facilities in Saudi Arabia for civil use. Trump later made the deal contingent on the U.S. ally establishing diplomatic relations with Israel by joining the Abraham Accords. The deal still needs to win congressional approval, but it raises ethics concerns. In December, Trump Media & Technology Group announced a $6 billion merger with the Taiwanese nuclear fusion company TAE Technologies, which plans to complete the world’s first utility-scale fusion power plant by 2031, despite hundreds of millions of dollars in losses by TMTG this year.

“We are at a point now that whenever the president announces a major official policy with a foreign government, a reasonable question arises of what's in it for him, and that knee-jerk reaction to ask if there's self-dealing shows how far we have come with lack of trust in government,” said Kedric Payne, the senior director of ethics at the nonpartisan Campaign Legal Center.

The Trump administration’s nuclear campaign kicked off last May, with the president signing four executive orders to streamline licensing processes, start a pilot program to test advanced nuclear reactors, and investigate the U.S.’s nuclear fuel supply.

Within three weeks of signing the executive orders, Trump acquired between $114,000 and $485,000 of stock in energy companies with nuclear facilities, including several five-figure purchases on the same day, the disclosure shows. His financial disclosure repeatedly shows dozens of single-day purchases of stock in everything from hotel groups and cosmetics companies to tech and energy businesses.

Trump’s stock portfolio includes investments in Vistra, Southern Company, Entergy, NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy, utilities that produce nuclear energy along with natural gas, solar energy, coal, and more.

White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said Trump’s assets are “held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions.” Trump has previously said that he does not communicate with the institutions in charge of his money.

“President Trump has unleashed a nuclear energy renaissance and reignited meaningful progress in America's nuclear power production,” Rogers said in a statement to NOTUS. “The media’s continued attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest are irresponsible and only deepen the public's distrust in what they read.”

The Trump Organization and the utility companies did not respond to NOTUS’ requests for comment.

The Biden administration, through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, reserved billions of dollars for funding nuclear projects to at least triple nuclear power generation by 2050. Former President Joe Biden pursued his own full-throttle energy agenda with billions of dollars and regulatory changes to grow the wind and solar industry as well.

Now, nuclear energy companies are benefiting from the Trump administration’s financial and policy support, which has thrust the industry to the fore as energy demand soars amid the data center buildout, and as the president deprioritizes other clean energy sources.

A month before the Saudi deal, the Department of Energy announced a $17.5 billion loan program for energy companies to purchase equipment that requires long lead times to secure. The equipment will be used to build up to ten commercial nuclear reactors jointly owned by the private power company Westinghouse, which last year reached an $80 billion agreement with the U.S. government to roll out reactors.

In January, the DOE announced $2.7 billion in contracts for U.S. companies developing enriched uranium to supply commercial nuclear reactors. The DOE has authorized 11 nuclear reactor testing projects through a pilot program announced in 2025. The DOE also launched a program to expand nuclear fuel supply chains and reduce U.S. reliance on enriched uranium and critical materials from abroad.

The pilot programs offer nuclear energy companies fast-tracked authorizations to build reactors and fuel production lines, with the possibility of later acquiring commercial licenses. Trump’s 2025 financial disclosure does not show investments in the 12 companies selected for the pilot programs, most of which are privately held.

The Trump administration’s bets are yielding some positive results. Days after the Saudi deal, the Trump administration announced that four advanced nuclear reactors reached criticality, the development stage when reactors can sustain a stable nuclear fission reaction.

entries.title: The DOJ Assails D.C. Council for Demanding National Guard Withdrawal
entries.summary: Administration officials say troops have contributed to historic drops in crime, but local officials contest that claim.
entries.content:
The Department of Justice on Wednesday acerbically accused the D.C. Council of “callousness” toward the city’s residents for sending letters to more than a dozen U.S. governors asking that they withdraw their National Guard troops by September 1.

“Let me be clear, your council has no power to demand that governors remove their brave men and women from serving in uniform in our Nation’s capital,” wrote Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald to the city’s lawmakers. “Your politically-motivated letter is impotent theatrics not worth the paper it’s written on, and D.C. is a much safer place no matter what you say.”

McDonald’s missive to the council — which was posted on social media — comes in the same week that the city marked a year since President Donald Trump deployed the National Guard in response to what he said were unacceptably high crime rates. It also stands as one of the administration’s loudest defenses of the Guard’s deployment, which is expected to continue through 2029.

“Directly coinciding with the assistance of the National Guard, the murder rate dropped substantially,” wrote McDonald. “To date, D.C. has seen the largest decline in violent crime in the history of the city, record safety for residents and tourists alike, the complete rehabilitation and beautification of the city’s history, monuments, and public spaces, and a total revitalization of the capital’s commercial and downtown regions.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“You might pretend violent crime isn’t down or act like the cause is unknown,” he continued. “But the public knows the city is safer. And honest people know why: on August 11, 2025, President Trump declared a crime emergency in D.C. and directed significant federal resources to protect life and liberty in the Nation’s capital. The results have been historic drops in violence.”

Earlier this week NOTUS reported that local reactions to the Guard’s continued deployment in D.C. have been mixed. Some residents say the troops are providing needed assistance and freeing local police up from menial tasks, while others say that having troops patrol the city’s neighborhoods sets a troubling precedent and could put people at risk should Trump order a more aggressive posture.

And while crime has generally declined over the past two years, many experts say that the McDonald’s argument that the National Guard is responsible mixes up causation and correlation. An analysis by the Niskanen Center found that the Guard’s presence may have helped contribute to a 24% decrease in property crimes, while not having much impact on violent crime.

Others say that the White House has skewed data to claim that its intervention with the National Guard has spurred declines in violent crime, even as cities across the U.S. were seeing such decreases before the president got involved. Historic drops in homicides and other violent crimes have occurred in Baltimore, just 40 miles north of D.C., without the same federal intervention D.C. has experienced.

Additionally, McDonald’s claims aren’t completely accurate. While homicides are down 33% from the same period last year, according to data maintained by the Metropolitan Police Department, overall violent crime is currently up 4% — driven largely by a 40% increase in assaults with a deadly weapon.

In their letters to the governors who have provided National Guard troops for the deployment in D.C., the council’s 13 members raised concerns over the cost of the ongoing mission.

“The deployment has … cost American taxpayers more than $3 million per day, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. Continuing this deployment despite the absence of a demonstrated violent-crime benefit would misuse both taxpayer dollars –— in the billions, if maintained for years at its expanded scale — and the service of the Guard members themselves,” they wrote. “[W]asting those resources on an ineffective, indefinite deployment that neither District residents nor officials asked for is disrespectful to American taxpayers.”

“In addition, the continued presence of military personnel in the nation’s capital through future election periods also risks normalizing the use of armed forces in and around spaces where residents vote, organize, protest, and participate in civic life. Whatever their stated mission, Guard personnel should not become a standing feature of the political and electoral landscape of the District,” they added.

McDonald closed his letter to the council by repeating a request that other administration officials have made over the last year: “You should withdraw your letters and dedicate your remaining time in public service to correcting D.C.’s laws to ensure criminals are punished and the public is protected — not the other way around.”

entries.title: Lawmakers Respond to Reports of Jaw-Dropping Conditions Aboard U.S. Aircraft Carrier
entries.summary: Concerns mounted after families described service members’ attempts to jump overboard.
entries.content:
Lawmakers are demanding answers after a series of jaw-dropping reports outlined what sailors and their families claimed were deteriorating conditions aboard an aircraft carrier, the USS Abraham Lincoln, which recently set the record for most consecutive days at sea without a port call.

The ship, which is supporting U.S. operations against Iran, left its home port in San Diego in November 2025 and has spent more than 250 days at sea. Concerns about the ship’s roughly 5,000 service members mounted after the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes published reports of family members describing suicidal ideation and food shortages on the Lincoln, with no apparent end in sight for its deployment.

Families said they were told that their relatives attempted to jump overboard or that other sailors had intervened to stop an attempt.

On the heels of those reports, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao in a letter this week to state what actions the Navy has taken to improve conditions.

The Connecticut Democrat blamed President Donald Trump and Hegseth’s management of the war against Iran for the situation, questioning whether the conflict was being carried out in a sustainable manner.

“These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force, particularly as this Administration repeatedly commits U.S. forces to conflicts of its own choosing and increasingly relies on aircraft carriers to sustain those operations,” Blumenthal wrote Wednesday.

He was one of a number of Democrats who demanded action from the White House.

Rep. Mike Levin of California called on Trump to remove Hegseth from his post, while Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a military veteran, wrote on X that the Navy must permit a bipartisan congressional delegation to board the Lincoln for an oversight investigation “into this horrible situation.”

Congressional delegations “have visited war zones to inspect the conditions of our troops,” Gallego wrote Wednesday. “There is no reason to be denied access.”

The Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reports of dire living conditions aboard the ship, and whether it planned to respond to Blumenthal’s letter.

In a statement to CNN, the Navy said it has not “observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship.”

“We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise,” the statement added.

entries.title: Carving Board
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 13, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

The Kennedy Center’s board voted to carve Donald Trump’s name into the building’s white marble facade, months after a judge ruled the president’s name had to be taken off the center’s signage.

  • The board, which Trump fired en masse last year and restocked with allies, also voted to proceed with shutting down the building for a $250 million renovation project.
The federal government investigated left-leaning groups during its immigration crackdown in Minnesota, according to a new filing in the U.S.’s case against a set of activists. Documents show Homeland Security officials used invasive tactics to investigate groups and individuals who were never accused of crimes.





THE ADMINISTRATION

The White House says the U.S. is losing up to $26 billion in annual tax revenue from tariff dodging, specifically highlighting how China responded to new import taxes in 2018 in a new report.

Todd Blanche tried to rally the DOJ troops in his first address to staff as attorney general.

  • “Everything that I do will not be the right path or the right decision,” he said, adding that he will listen to staff suggestions and make adjustments accordingly.
  • The agency assailed the D.C. Council for demanding more than a dozen U.S. governors withdraw their National Guard troops by Sept. 1.




THE HILL

Lawmakers are demanding answers after reports of deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln. The USS George Washington carrier group is headed to the Middle East to replace the aircraft carrier in a previously planned swap, according to CNN.

  • Reports about poor conditions were “completely misrepresented,” Hegseth told reporters in Panama today.
Chatbots are doing the work of Congress with little oversight, The Washington Post reports.

  • “It’s kind of like you can sit there and talk to an expert,” Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama) said of his experience with ChatGPT. “You don’t know whether or not they’re 100 percent correct. But they put you on the right path.”

entries.title: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Carve Trump’s Name Into the Building’s Marble Facade
entries.summary: The decision appears to be aimed at circumventing a federal judge’s order to remove separate signage bearing the president’s name.
entries.content:
The Kennedy Center’s board voted Thursday to inscribe President Donald Trump’s name into the storied building’s white marble facade and proceed with a lengthy shutdown of the venue to accommodate an extensive $250 million renovation project, according to ex officio member Rep. Joyce Beatty.

The decision comes just months after a judge ruled that separate signage bearing the president’s name had to be taken off the building’s marquee. The new inscription will test the order, though due to ongoing litigation the judge has the power to delay the projects.

The board, which Trump fired en masse last year and restocked with allies, voted to close the center’s main building, while The Reach, a newer expansion to the facility, will remain open for limited events. It will also serve as a memorial to former President John F. Kennedy.

The president announced the renovations in February and said the center would need to close for two years.

An outside consulting firm concluded that keeping the main building open during the construction project would be significantly more expensive. The board reviewed a 163-page plan for the $250 million renovation project ahead of the meeting, according to The New York Times.

The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new inscription, which is set to read “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump,” will be placed under the marquee bearing President John F. Kennedy’s name, according to Beatty. The board also approved a motion to rename the physical site on which the center stands to “The President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

Following Thursday’s meeting, Beatty lashed out at the Kennedy Center board members who green-lit the changes.

“This morning’s decision to close the Center and the surprise agenda item to put Donald Trump’s name back on the building was more of the same,” Beatty wrote in a statement. “This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed. I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”

Trump’s push to renovate the Kennedy Center — including affixing his name to the front marble exterior — has launched several monthslong court battles and prompted congressional scrutiny over funding for the renovations.

Trump’s handpicked board had initially sought to rebrand the center and place his name on top of Kennedy’s, dubbing the institution the “Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.”

But U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued an opinion in May that blocked the proposed renovation project and halted the center’s renaming in response to a lawsuit filed by Beatty.

Cooper ruled that the board had been “derelict” by neglecting the potential impact the renovation could have on the programming at the center.

Trump railed against Cooper’s decision at the time, calling him a “Highly Conflicted, Crooked Federal Judge” and saying the Kennedy Center is “broken, unsafe, and busted,” in a post on Truth Social in May.

The Trump-backed renovations at the Kennedy Center come amid a wave of beautification projects at government buildings across D.C. — including the addition of a large ballroom at White House and the refurbishment of historic landmarks like the Reflecting Pool.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: The U.S. Surveilled Left-Leaning Groups During Immigration Crackdown in Minnesota
entries.summary: Government agencies targeted protesters in two sweeping surveillance operations, new federal court filings show.
entries.content:
Homeland Security officials secretly spied on and investigated progressive groups and protesters during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, new court filings show.

The motion for discovery, filed in the U.S.’s ongoing federal case against local activists, details two undercover surveillance operations that targeted protesters and dissidents during and following the Homeland Security Department’s January descent into the Twin Cities.

Through “Operation Puppet Master” and “Project Whipple Shield,” undercover agents attended community meetings across the capital region, covertly recorded conversations and obtained financial records — all without any basis for suspecting criminal activity. Attorneys who represent the 15 people charged with conspiring to impede or injure federal agents say the usage of such surveillance tactics on those practicing political dissent violated the First Amendment.

DHS officials conducted these operations under a directive President Donald Trump signed last September that tasked that agency and the Justice Department with investigating individuals and groups under an expanded definition of domestic terrorism.

Operation Puppet Master was opened four days after federal immigration agents fatally shot Alex Pretti while he filmed officers detaining a woman. Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh used Trump’s September memo to encourage officials and prosecutors to pursue a sweeping set of cases that could generate headlines, The New York Times reported in March.

“Go big and go loud,” Singh said at the time.

One exhibit features a PowerPoint diagram of 18 organizations — including Twin Cities Democratic Socialists of America, Minnesota ICE Watch and labor union chapters like the AFL-CIO — that Homeland Security Investigations alleges were conspiring to interfere with the work of federal immigration agents in the state.

DHS reports lay out plans to investigate “funding sources, organizational structures and predicate actions” for those organizations and others, over two dozen filings show, even before agents had identified any specific criminal basis to do so.

Agents subpoenaed wire transfer information from the labor union SEIU and donation information from Voices for Racial Justice. Some tailed three of the defendants for a day in March. Others recorded panel discussions and team meetings to detail the ways protesters and dissidents planned to combat immigration officers stationed in the Twin Cities while evading breaking the law.

During a Sunrise Movement-Twin Cities meeting, one agent recorded possible actions members would take against immigration officers, including “shaming and bullying ICE” or “wasting ICE’s resources such as flooding their tipline and taking long time [sic] during interviews.” That agent embedded themselves in an operational planning group chat, a June investigation report details.

“These agents surreptitiously recorded dozens of conversations with ordinary people who were simply exercising their First Amendment right to protest ICE’s lawless rampage in our state,” Kevin Riach, the attorney who filed the motion for discovery, wrote. “The agents gathered information about Minnesotans from law enforcement databases and internet searches, and created dossiers that are apparently now available agency-wide.”

The documents, filed in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, are part of a broader request for more information regarding the investigation and the undercover agents who participated. In his motion for discovery, Riach asked the government for more relevant documents — including about an “Operation Keyhole” mentioned in an opening report, under which the first case was accepted — and internal agency communications.
